summary: Saul, "yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord," secures letters for Damascus to bring "any of this way" bound to Jerusalem. Near the city "suddenly there shined round about him a light from heaven"; he falls and hears, "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" He asks, "Who art thou, Lord?", and is answered, "I am Jesus whom thou persecutest," then told to go where "it shall be told thee what thou must do." Blind three days and fasting, he prays. The Lord sends the disciple Ananias, who objects to Saul's "much evil" against the saints; the Lord replies, "he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel," and adds, "I will shew him how great things he must suffer for my name’s sake." Ananias lays hands on him, calls him "Brother Saul," and "immediately there fell from his eyes as it had been scales"; he sees, is baptized, and "straightway he preached Christ in the synagogues, that he is the Son of God." Amazement turns to plotting, and the disciples let him down "by the wall in a basket." At Jerusalem they fear him until Barnabas brings him to the apostles. With the churches at rest and "multiplied," Peter travels: at Lydda he tells palsied Æneas, "Jesus Christ maketh thee whole: arise, and make thy bed," and at Joppa he prays over the dead Tabitha, says, "Tabitha, arise," and presents her alive, so that "many believed in the Lord."
takeaways: Christ identifies himself with his persecuted disciples — "why persecutest thou me?" — so that the Church is not merely a group that follows him but a body joined to him, and what is done to the least of its members is done to the Lord himself.

Grace here is sheer initiative. Saul is stopped in the middle of his errand, given no room to bargain, and named "a chosen vessel"; the vocation includes suffering from the first announcement of it, not as a later disappointment.

The convert is not left as a private visionary. The risen Lord who could have finished the work on the road instead sends him to Ananias, to sight and baptism, and afterward through Barnabas to the apostles, so an extraordinary call is verified within the ordinary community.

Peter's healing of Æneas and raising of Tabitha are done in Christ's name and out of prayer, presenting apostolic works as continuations of the Lord's own; Tabitha's "good works and almsdeeds" name the kind of life the Church grieves over and God restores.

crossRefs.label: Acts 22:6-16 — Paul retells his conversion before the crowd in Jerusalem
crossRefs.why: Paul's own account adds his question, "What shall I do, Lord?", and Ananias' charge, "arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins, calling on the name of the Lord." It fills in what Acts 9 compresses and shows that Saul understood the encounter as a commission from the start.

crossRefs.label: Galatians 1:13-24 — Paul's own account of his past and his calling
crossRefs.why: Paul admits that "beyond measure I persecuted the church of God," says he went into Arabia before Jerusalem, and reports the churches' words, "he which persecuted us in times past now preacheth the faith which once he destroyed." Reading it beside Acts 9 shows the same conversion told from inside, with a different interest in chronology.

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 11:32-33 — let down by the wall in a basket at Damascus
crossRefs.why: Paul recalls that the governor under Aretas watched the city for him and that "through a window in a basket was I let down by the wall, and escaped his hands." He lists it among his humiliations rather than his exploits, which colors the escape in Acts 9 as a beginning in weakness.

crossRefs.label: 1 Timothy 1:12-16 — the persecutor who obtained mercy as a pattern
crossRefs.why: Paul calls himself "a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious" who obtained mercy, and "of whom I am chief" among sinners, saying he was shown longsuffering "for a pattern to them which should hereafter believe." It reads Acts 9 as a template of mercy rather than a singular exception.

crossRefs.label: Mark 5:35-43 — Jesus takes the dead girl by the hand and says Talitha cumi
crossRefs.why: Jesus puts the mourners out, takes the child's hand, and says, "Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise." Peter at Joppa repeats the shape of the scene almost gesture for gesture, but kneels to pray first, marking his power as borrowed rather than his own.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition the words "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" are read as revealing the Church as the body of Christ, so that the visible community of disciples is so united to him that attacking it is attacking him, which grounds the Catholic conviction that the Church is not an optional association added to faith but the form Christ's own life takes in the world.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally affirm the same union with Christ wholeheartedly, but read the identification as covenantal solidarity with all who trust him rather than as a claim about one visible institution, holding that the body is constituted by faith in Christ and includes believers wherever they are found. On this reading the verse comforts the persecuted more than it settles questions of church order. Both traditions agree that Christ counts harm done to his people as done to himself, and that no one meets him while opposing those who belong to him.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading gives weight to the sending of Ananias: the risen Lord, who has just appeared in person, still directs Saul into a city to wait for a disciple who lays hands on him and after which he is baptized, which is taken as a pattern of grace ordinarily reaching people through the ministry and sacraments of the Church rather than around them.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read Ananias as an instrument God freely chose, noting that the decisive encounter happened on the road with no human agent present and that God is never bound to the means he graciously uses. They often emphasize instead that Ananias' visit gave the frightened community a witness to what had really happened to their persecutor. Both traditions agree that God deliberately involved the Church in Saul's restoration, and that his calling was confirmed and received by the community rather than kept as a private matter between him and the Lord.
